extract:
Bruce Springsteen was born in 1949 in Long Branch, New Jersey, and raised in nearby Freehold, a working-class town whose factories, Catholic schools, and main-street disappointments would later furnish the imagery of his songs. He emerged from the Jersey Shore bar scene of the late 1960s and early 1970s, particularly the boardwalk clubs of Asbury Park, where he played in groups like Steel Mill and the Bruce Springsteen Band before signing with Columbia Records in 1972 under the guidance of John Hammond, the legendary A&R man who had previously signed Bob Dylan. His active recording career has now spanned more than five decades.

His formative influences ran from Elvis Presley and the early rock and roll he watched on the Ed Sullivan Show, through the Brill Building pop of Roy Orbison and Phil Spector's wall of sound, to Dylan's verbose songwriting and the soul revues of the 1960s. His first two albums, Greetings from Asbury Park, N.J. and The Wild, the Innocent and the E Street Shuffle, both released in 1973, were verbose, jazz-inflected, and commercially modest, though they cemented the lineup that would become the E Street Band, including saxophonist Clarence Clemons, pianist Roy Bittan, organist Danny Federici, drummer Max Weinberg, bassist Garry Tallent, and guitarist Steven Van Zandt. Born to Run, released in 1975 and co-produced with Jon Landau and Mike Appel, was the breakthrough, landing him simultaneously on the covers of Time and Newsweek and reframing him as the great romantic chronicler of American escape.

A protracted legal dispute with Appel kept him out of the studio until Darkness on the Edge of Town in 1978, a leaner and grimmer record that began his shift toward themes of class, labor, and constraint. The double album The River followed in 1980, yielding his first top-ten single in Hungry Heart, and was succeeded by the stark solo home recording Nebraska in 1982, made on a four-track cassette machine. Born in the U.S.A., released in 1984, became a cultural phenomenon, producing seven top-ten singles and selling tens of millions of copies, though its title track was widely misread as patriotic anthem rather than veteran's lament. He dissolved the E Street Band at the end of the 1980s, recording Tunnel of Love and the simultaneously released Human Touch and Lucky Town in a more introspective register.

Springsteen reconvened the E Street Band around the turn of the millennium, and The Rising in 2002, produced by Brendan O'Brien, framed the September 11 attacks in collective, communal terms. He has since alternated between band records like Magic and Wrecking Ball, folk excursions such as We Shall Overcome: The Seeger Sessions, and more personal projects including Western Stars and Letter to You. His memoir Born to Run appeared in 2016, the same year he launched Springsteen on Broadway, an extended solo theatrical run that won a special Tony Award.

He has been inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, received the Kennedy Center Honors and the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and recently toured internationally with the E Street Band into the mid-2020s, his stature as the foremost rock chronicler of American working life essentially uncontested.
title: Bruce Springsteen
